AI in health policy often swings between hype (“it will fix shortages”) and fear (“it will automate clinicians”), but most real deployments are narrower: decision support, documentation, triage, scheduling, claims, and other workflow layers where a small error rate can still have large consequences. This piece is a useful reset for policymakers who need to evaluate proposals without becoming model experts.

The key framing is to treat AI as a system, not a widget. That means insisting on evidence that matches the intended use (and population), clear accountability when things go wrong, and ongoing monitoring after rollout. In practice, that translates into concrete questions: what data does the tool rely on; what happens when data shifts; how are errors detected and surfaced; how is human oversight designed; and what procurement clauses (audit rights, update policies, data retention) are needed so governance isn’t an afterthought.

If you’re trying to sanity-check a proposal quickly, it’s also a helpful reminder to separate “model quality” from “deployment quality.” A strong benchmark number doesn’t tell you how the system behaves in your setting, how updates are rolled out, or whether the organization can actually detect and learn from mistakes.
